title: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: contemporary classification, molecular pathology, and emerging concepts
abstractText: Abstract Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is an aggressive primary liver malignancy with poor outcome. It is characterized by heterogeneous clinicopathological features as well as molecular landscapes. The updated World Health Organization (WHO) classification system underscores the critical distinction between small-duct and large-duct types, which exhibit distinct morphologic patterns, immunohistochemical profiles, molecular alterations, and clinical outcomes. Besides, rare and unique morphologic subtypes of iCCA continue to challenge diagnostic and treatment paradigms. This review provides an overview of the 2026 WHO classification and evolving concepts in iCCA, with a particular emphasis on the practical application of immunohistochemical and emerging molecular biomarkers essential for an accurate diagnosis and guiding targeted therapies. Furthermore, this manuscript addresses contemporary controversies and unresolved emerging practical issues with iCCA that are reshaping personalized therapeutic strategies and prognostication.

title: Comparison of the neural recovery effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy according to administration time in sciatic nerve-injured rats
abstractText: Abstract Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) has been reported to promote peripheral nerve regeneration but whether its efficacy is maintained when treatment is initiated after the acute phase remains unclear. This study compared the neuroregenerative effects of immediate and delayed ESWT in a rat sciatic nerve crush model. Sixty rats were assigned to immediate treatment ([IT]; ESWT immediately after injury), delayed treatment ([DT]; ESWT 7 days postinjury), control, and sham groups. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy was delivered at an energy flux density of 0.19 mJ mm−². Molecular, structural, and functional outcomes were evaluated for 9 weeks. Both IT and DT groups showed higher expression of glial fibrillary acidic protein, S100β, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, growth-associated protein 43, and NF200 than the control group. Histomorphometric analysis showed comparable improvements in axonal area and remyelination. At 9 weeks, G-ratios were lower in the IT (0.59 ± 0.04) and DT (0.60 ± 0.02) groups than in the control group (0.69 ± 0.02; both P < .05), with no difference between the treatment groups. Compound muscle action potentials [CMAP] amplitudes at week 9 were higher in the IT (39.5 ± 2.6 mV) and DT (40.1 ± 3.0 mV) groups than the control group (33.3 ± 2.5 mV; both P < .05). Immediate and delayed ESWT were associated with improved nerve regeneration, supporting the biological efficacy of ESWT initiated 7 days postinjury in this sciatic nerve crush model.

Intermittent Fasting in Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Evidence, Molecular Mechanisms, and Future Perspectives
abstractText: Abstract The objective for this narrative review was to synthesize and critically assess the clinical evidence, molecular mechanisms, and future directions of intermittent fasting (IF) for managing metabolic syndrome (MetS). Metabolic syndrome is a complex cardiometabolic disorder associated with abnormal dietary patterns, epigenetic regulation, and gene activity, and characterized by central adiposity, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Intermittent fasting regimens, including time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting, and the 5:2 fasting regimen, are promising nutritional interventions. Nonetheless, large, randomized trials have reported mixed clinical outcomes, and critical uncertainties persist regarding clinical effectiveness, molecular mechanisms, and whether benefits arise from fasting timing or weight-loss-driven energy restriction. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in major databases through July 2026. Articles, including those reporting on randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant preclinical mechanistic investigations in MetS, were selected and their data synthesized. Findings show that certain IF regimens produce modest improvements in body weight, waist circumference, and selected cardiometabolic risk markers; however, effects on glycemic control, lipid profiles, and liver-related end points are heterogeneous across trials. Observed clinical responses vary by fasting protocol, participant phenotype, and adherence, and high-quality human mechanistic data remain limited. Mechanistic insights, largely derived from preclinical models, highlight circadian rhythm synchronization and nutrient-sensing network modulation as key biological pathways. Important unresolved controversies cover protocol optimization, long-term adherence, and inter-individual metabolic variability. Intermittent fasting may serve as a feasible nonpharmacological adjunct intervention for MetS and related conditions, yet existing evidence is inconsistent. Translation toward precision lifestyle medicine requires resolution of ongoing controversies, improved evaluation of evidence quality, development of personalized fasting protocols, and rigorous assessment of long-term safety and sustainability across diverse patient populations.

abstractText: We consider the flow of a gravity current released from a lock inside a tank which performs horizontal oscillations (equivalent to internal pressure-gradient pulses), in the buoyancy–inertia (high-Reynolds-number) regime. We develop a shallow-water model which provides clear-cut insights and simple predictions of the propagation, height and velocity fields as a function of time, for a wide range of parameters. Comparisons with the simulations of Bingol et al. (2025 J. Fluid. Mech. , vol. 1002, A14) support the approximate analysis. Moreover, we point out a new effect, called pulse-buoyancy, which was not covered by these simulation. The clear-cut predictions of the model are amenable to straightforward experimental verification, and suggest further numerical work for an as yet unexplored parameter range.

title: Perspectives of those with lived and professional experience on vision rehabilitation and related supports in Ghana: a descriptive qualitative study
abstractText: Abstract Background Approximately 90% of people with unaddressed vision impairment or blindness live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Ghana. While access to vision rehabilitation, education, assistive devices, eye care services and government-supported programs can improve independence and social inclusion of people with visual impairment (PVI), research seldom documents how these individuals navigate such supports in real life. This study explored the perspectives of PVI, optometrists (OD), and rehabilitation practitioners and educators (R&E) on vision rehabilitation and associated support structures for PVI in Ghana. Methods Using a descriptive qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 participants, namely 4 PVI, 3 R&E, and 3 OD. Participants were purposively sampled across three stakeholder groups. PVI were recruited through circulation of the study invitation by the Ghana Blind Union and participant referrals, optometrists through the first author’s professional network, and R&E participants through snowball sampling between November 2024 and March 2025. A semi-structured interview guide was adapted from prior research. All interviews were conducted via Zoom, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed thematically in MAXQDA. Results Inductive thematic analysis led to the development of seven themes, namely: Resources as a pathway to independence, Living with fragmented support, Knowledge barriers in accessing support, Compromised safety, Financial and structural burden of visual disability, Stigma and social exclusion, and Call for reform. From participants’ responses, vocational training, peer networks, inclusive education, and free assistive devices were perceived as beneficial, whereas barriers including inconsistent service provision, environmental inaccessibility, poor public awareness, and perceived gaps in the implementation of disability policies were reported. Conclusion The findings point to a gap between the resources available to support PVI and the barriers that may limit their access. When considered alongside previous research, closing this gap may involve the Government of Ghana prioritising the integration of vision rehabilitation into the eye care system, increasing public awareness, expanding support systems, and reinforcing the implementation of disability policies, in close collaboration with PVI and the professionals who support them, to promote the well-being of PVI.

title: Analytical modelling of STIX instrumental background and its application in the spectral and imaging analysis
abstractText: Abstract STIX records X-rays from Solar activity from 4 to 150 keV with 32 detectors, each divided into 12 pixels. Background is obtained using the BKG detector and is known to essentially correspond to the background radioactive sources onboard STIX. This study aims to construct an analytical model of the STIX background based on available measures. The model will allow predicting the background at any time interval of the mission. We analysed 256 background files recorded by STIX from January 2022 to July 2023, and we assume that onboard calibration sources ( $$^{133}$$ Ba) dominate the background. We fitted with an exponential function corresponding to the half-life of $$^{133}$$ Ba to the background in each of the 384 pixels and each of the science energy bins. Interpolated background values were validated against additional files for consistency. These values were then integrated into image reconstruction algorithms to assess variability in source parameters across background approaches. A determined background was also tested in OSPEX to evaluate its impact on spectral fitting. The analysis shows that the STIX background is non-uniform, with pixel-to-pixel variations affecting moiré patterns in weak flares. Our approximation matches background files collected during quiet Sun periods, but it can also differ from them during high activity or perihelion, where onboard files include additional signals. In such cases, our radioactive-source-based background offers a more reliable basis for imaging and spectral analysis than file-based background and enables a higher degree of automation in the analysis. Background analysis from Jan 2022 to Jul 2023 shows that STIX background is usually dominated by $$^{133}$$ Ba over the full energy spectrum. Interpolated background methods improve accuracy during high solar activity or close Sun approaches, where standard methods falter. This enhances X-ray image quality and enables reconstruction from fewer counts, supporting more precise analyses, especially of microflares.

title: VSTAR-G: Cloud-Based Tool for Global Detection and Quantification of Volcanic SO2 Plumes Using TROPOMI and Machine Learning Approach
abstractText: SO2 emissions are among the primary indicators of magmatic activity and play a fundamental role both in local-scale risk management, including air quality and aviation safety, and in regional-to-global climate processes through the formation of sulfate aerosols capable of altering the Earth’s radiative balance. In recent years, satellite observations have revolutionized the monitoring of volcanic emissions. In particular, the Sentinel-5P satellite, part of the Copernicus programme, carries the TROPOMI spectrometer, which provides high-resolution observations for monitoring of atmospheric trace gases (e.g., SO2). Here, we present VSTAR-G, a Google Earth Engine (GEE) application that operationalizes an algorithm previously developed. The application is able to visualize and analyse, using an algorithm previously developed, the automatic detection of volcanic SO2 plumes and their mass quantification according to plume altitude. Through an intuitive interface, users can interactively explore SO2 emissions from more than 200 volcanoes worldwide, define spatial and temporal regions of interest (ROIs), and compare different dates or plume-height products using a synchronized split-window visualization. The application also generates time series of the SO2 mass within the selected area, supports the simultaneous analysis of multiple plumes, and allows users to export plume-detection maps in GeoTIFF format and the associated satellite data as CSV files. The developed application transforms an existing detection algorithm into an accessible operational tool, combining satellite observations, machine learning, and cloud computing to support scalable and near-real-time monitoring of volcanic SO2 emissions.

A High-Brightness, Low-Energy-Spread Au Needle Point Electron Source Nanocold-Cathode Adapted to Low-Power Photoelectric Coexcitation
abstractText: Abstract To address the requirements of vacuum electronic and optoelectronic device applications for next-generation low-power-consumption, high-brightness, low-energy-spread, and tunable electron sources, the pursuit of high-efficiency metal nanocold-cathodes with plasmon-enhanced properties in specific waveband emerges as one of potent solutions. In this study, by screening and comparing the cathode materials and structures, we propose a high-brightness, low-energy-spread Au needle nanocold-cathode point electron source adapted to low-intensity photoelectric coexcitation. The experimental results demonstrate sensitivity to excitation light and outstanding electron emission performance of this point electron source: under the coexcitation of an electrostatic field below ∼1.25 V μm–1 and a supercontinuum-spectrum laser with average intensity of ∼24 W cm–2, the source achieved an emission current of 130 nA, improving by one order of magnitude when compared to the field emission current (∼13 nA) under pure electrostatic field excitation. As the laser excitation intensity increased, its effective work function decreased from 5.1 to 2.7 eV, resulting in a significant reduction of the excitation threshold for electron emission. Benefiting from the plasmon-enhanced light-harvesting effect, the cathode exhibits high sensitivity and selectivity to the wavelength and polarization of the incident light. In the 532–675 nm plasmon resonance band, the emission current exceeds 225 nA at an average excitation intensity of only 7.05 W cm–2, ∼17 times the pure electrostatic field emission current. Meanwhile, the plasmon relaxation preferentially populates high-energy electrons and suppresses the energy spread broadening induced by the space charge effect, thereby achieving a high reduced brightness of 6.89 × 109 A m–2 sr–1 V–1 and a low-energy spread of approximately 0.5 eV. This low-power photoelectric coexcitation scheme greatly relaxes the requirements on the excitation source, providing a route for the miniaturization and integration of vacuum optoelectronic point electron sources.

abstractText: Abstract Purpose Glaucoma is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy and one of the leading causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Beyond visual impairment, the disease can impose a considerable psychological burden. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between glaucoma and psychological distress, and to identify clinical and psychosocial predictors that may contribute to heightened risk, with the aim of informing management strategies to improve patients’ quality of life. Methods A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted involving 107 glaucoma patients treated at the University Eye Clinic Cologne. Data were collected using a standardized questionnaire, including demographic and clinical variables as well as the validated Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, and multiple linear regression to identify predictors of psychological burden. Results 25.23% of patients exhibited mild to severe depressive symptoms according to PHQ-9 scores. Significant predictors of higher psychological burden were increased disease preoccupation (β = 0.237, p = 0.007), stronger fear of blindness (β = 0.315, p < 0.001), and poorer self-rated general health status (β = -0.382, p < 0.001). Conclusion The findings demonstrate a strong link between glaucoma and psychological distress. These results highlight the need to consider psychosocial factors alongside intraocular pressure in glaucoma management. Interdisciplinary care involving ophthalmologists, psychologists, and nursing staff may improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: In vitro comparison of Aβ-targeting SNIPR, synNotch, and TRUCK for programmable transgene expression
abstractText: Abstract Background Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) are being used to direct cytokine secretion and phagocytosis by immune and glial cells toward amyloid β (Aβ) pathology, effectively adapting oncology-derived cell therapies to Alzheimer’s disease (AD). New synthetic receptor systems can take this approach a step further by enabling cells to deliver genetically encoded therapeutics. Among these systems, T cells Redirected for Universal Cytokine Killing (TRUCKs), synthetic Notch (synNotch), and Synthetic Intramembrane Proteolysis Receptors (SNIPRs) have shown promise in oncology and, as CARs, could potentially be adapted to AD. Methods Here, we compared these receptor systems in vitro using Jurkat cells and human regulatory T cells (Tregs). All receptors shared an Aβ-targeting binding domain derived from Aducanumab (Aduhelm) and were coupled to inducible expression cassettes driving identical transgenes: secreted Metridia luciferase (MetLuc) and a Lecanemab (Leqembi)-based chimeric human–mouse antibody (chLecanemab). To model AD pathology in vitro, cell clones were exposed to oligomer-enriched Aβ (AβO) preparations. In Jurkat cells, TRUCK, synNotch, and SNIPR systems were assessed for basal transcriptional leakage, ligand-independent activation, and ligand-dependent activation using flow cytometry and MetLuc reporter assays. Aβ-dependent production of chLecanemab by synNotch and SNIPR systems was further evaluated in Jurkat cells and human Tregs by immunofluorescence (IF). Results We found that the inducible expression cassettes of all receptor systems exhibited transcriptional leakage. Despite confirmed CAR function and transcriptional competence of 6xNFAT response elements paired with different minimal promoters, none of the TRUCK variants produced AβO-induced output significantly above basal leakage. In contrast, synNotch and SNIPR expressed in Jurkat cells and human Tregs responded robustly to AβO. Conclusions We demonstrate that Aβ-targeting SNIPR and synNotch systems can support Aβ-dependent inducible transgene expression in vitro. Their modular architectures enable straightforward substitution of chLecanemab with alternative therapeutic payloads while preserving Aβ-dependent delivery. Because these receptors are orthogonal, the same sequences we provide can be used across different model species and cell types in further studies without requiring receptor redesign.

title: Differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells into articular chondrocytes: advances, challenges, and future directions
abstractText: Cartilage injury and osteoarthritis-associated degeneration remain major clinical challenges because articular cartilage is avascular, aneural, and alymphatic, leaving it with limited intrinsic capacity for repair. Current clinical strategies, including microfracture, osteochondral grafting, autologous chondrocyte implantation, and mesenchymal stem cell-based approaches, can relieve symptoms and partially restore tissue architecture. However, these approaches, particularly mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies, often produce fibrocartilage rather than durable hyaline cartilage and do not reliably reproduce the long-term mechanical competence or molecular identity of native articular cartilage. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a promising alternative cell source for cartilage regeneration because they combine unlimited self-renewal with the capacity to generate patient-specific or allogeneic chondroprogenitors, articular chondrocytes, cartilage organoids, and engineered cartilage constructs. iPSC-derived chondrocytes also provide versatile platforms for modeling osteoarthritis and genetic skeletal disorders, performing genome editing, testing disease-modifying drugs, and developing personalized tissue-engineering systems. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by protocol variability, incomplete lineage specification, hypertrophic differentiation, residual pluripotent cells, immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, biomechanical immaturity, and the need for scalable Good Manufacturing Practice-compliant manufacturing. This review summarizes the developmental principles and molecular signaling networks that guide iPSC chondrogenesis, compares current differentiation and tissue-engineering strategies, and discusses therapeutic applications and key barriers that must be addressed to achieve safe, reproducible, and clinically effective iPSC-based cartilage repair.

Nocebo effect of nintedanib on gastrointestinal events in interstitial lung diseases
abstractText: Abstract Background Nintedanib is known to be associated with gastrointestinal adverse events including diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting. We investigated whether a nocebo effect (an unfavourable effect that may be attributed to expectation) may have contributed to the gastrointestinal adverse events reported in clinical trials of nintedanib in patients with interstitial lung diseases (ILDs). Methods Using data from the placebo groups of trials of nintedanib in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) (TOMORROW, INPULSIS), systemic sclerosis-associated ILD (SENSCIS) and progressive fibrosing ILDs other than IPF (INBUILD), we analysed rates of gastrointestinal adverse events in the on-treatment period and the post-discontinuation period. Results In TOMORROW, rates per 100 patient-years of diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, respectively, were 19.8, 11.4 and 5.5 in the on-treatment period, and 0, 0 and 0 in the post-discontinuation period. In INPULSIS, rates per 100 patient-years of diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, respectively, were 23.1, 7.6 and 2.9 in the on-treatment period and 2.4, 2.4 and 0 in the post-discontinuation period. In SENSCIS, rates per 100 patient-years of diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, respectively, were 33.1, 11.8 and 9.0 in the on-treatment period and 19.1, 2.4 and 7.4 in the post-discontinuation period. In INBUILD, rates per 100 patient-years of diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, respectively, were 23.3, 7.7 and 3.6 in the on-treatment period and 2.2, 9.5 and 0 in the post-discontinuation period. Conclusions In trials of nintedanib in patients with ILDs, the rates of gastrointestinal adverse events fell after placebo was discontinued, suggesting the possibility of a nocebo effect. Trial registration The trials were prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov with identifier numbers NCT00514683 (TOMORROW), NCT01335464 and NCT01335477 (INPULSIS), NCT02597933 (SENSCIS) and NCT02999178 (INBUILD).

Polyurethane Recycling Using Catalytic Pyrolysis: Insights into Catalyst Stability
abstractText: Abstract Polyurethanes are widely used in many applications because of their versatility. However, efficient recycling remains challenging. Recent findings indicate that aniline recovery from rigid polyurethane foams via catalytic pyrolysis with an alumina-based catalyst is an attractive option. Techno-economic analyses showed that catalyst costs are a major factor and that catalyst recycling is essential. Here, we report an extensive study on the recyclability of a selected alumina-based catalyst (Puralox 5/200) for the catalytic pyrolysis of PUR. Experiments with fresh and spent catalysts in a batch-operated staged free-fall reactor at gram scale (3.0 g nPUR, catalyst-to-feed ratio: 1 to 1, 550 °C) using virgin PUR showed differences in activity and chemoselectivity for aniline, indicative of catalyst deactivation. Spent catalyst characterization (TGA–MS, TEM–EDX, N2 physisorption, TPD, and XRD) showed hard coke (14.4 wt %) on the catalyst. Catalyst regeneration was successfully demonstrated using an oxidative treatment at 550 °C, though some irreversible deactivation, including loss in acidity and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area, as well as inorganic accumulation, was observed after five regeneration/recycles. Additional experiments to assess catalyst performance after multiple regeneration-recycles were carried out on a milligram scale in a tandem microreactor coupled to GC–MS/FID (catalyst-to-feed ratio of 5:1 at 550 °C), using rigid polyurethane (nPUR) and a contaminated end-of-life (EOL) feed. With nPUR, catalyst performance for aniline and toluidine formation declined in the first 4 cycles, then stabilized at half the original activity for 28 cycles, and finally dropped to very low levels. For EOL PUR, catalyst performance over multiple runs was significantly worse, and the catalyst was inactive after 18 cycles. We characterized the spent catalysts from both PUR feeds (a.o TEM–EDX), which showed that inorganic impurity accumulation contributes to catalyst deactivation.

Academic self-condemnation, maladaptive emotion regulation, and NSSI-related risk cognition in chinese adolescents: a three-wave cohort study
abstractText: Abstract Background Academic pressure is a salient developmental context in Chinese adolescence, but longitudinal evidence is limited on how academic difficulty is internalized as shame-based self-evaluation and linked to later non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) risk cognition. Methods The study involved 3,734 secondary school students from Zhejiang Province, China, of whom 2,915 completed assessments at baseline (T1), 6 months (T2), and 12 months (T3). The primary complete-case analysis included 2,854 adolescents across 134 classes. We examined the prospective relationships from T1 shame and guilt proneness to T2 academic self-evaluative burden and cognitive emotion regulation, as well as from these T2 variables to T3 future likelihood of NSSI, conceptualized as NSSI-related risk cognition. Results T1 Shame-NSE was associated with higher T2 academic self-evaluative burden (β = 0.102, 95% CI [0.066, 0.138]). Academic burden was contemporaneously associated with catastrophizing (β = 0.176, 95% CI [0.133, 0.220]) and self-blame (β = 0.234, 95% CI [0.191, 0.277]), and all three T2 constructs were independently associated with higher T3 self-reported future NSSI likelihood (ORs = 1.19–1.22). Shame-Withdraw, the guilt facets, and rumination showed no independent T3 associations in simultaneous models. In the exploratory behavioral analysis, academic burden was also associated with newly reported T3 past-year NSSI (OR = 1.40, 95% CI [1.09, 1.79]). Conclusions The findings refine broad academic-pressure accounts by identifying academic self-condemnation as a domain-specific correlate of later NSSI-related risk cognition, alongside self-blame and catastrophizing. This pattern offers a testable school-linked formulation hypothesis.
